item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Man n and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode. For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors. In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:03) Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register 's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter. Welcome guys. Tobias Mann (00:34) Good to be here. Tom Claburn (00:34) Good to be here. Brandon (00:36) So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb . Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO. Tobias Mann (00:56) Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy. Brandon (01:18) Right. Tobias Mann (01:18) The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars. Brandon (01:40) I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported. Tobias Mann (01:46) Right. Brandon (01:47) Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically? Tobias Mann (02:01) Not specifically. It's a little fuzzy, and it's always kind of like this. Brandon (02:07) Of course it is, right? Tobias Mann (02:09) Anthropic's business is extremely cash heavy, and so they had to go to partners and say, "Hey, we need capital in order to pay for compute to train these models. We can either take it in debt or you could also get repaid in valuation, our equity." And so I believe a large part of that loss is they're trying to write off a lot of the equity that they're going to have to pay off when they do go public. And so I do believe that's the lion's share of that loss. Because it does look huge, but when you think about how companies go public and how they raise capital as startups, it's not really that surprising. It's just a huge number because Anthropic is arguably the largest IPO in US history at this point. Brandon (03:02) Right. But bottom line is their actual day-to-day business losses were $693 million....It was $1.2 billion, I think, for the first half of the year or same time last year or something like that. So it's gone down. Tobias Mann (03:17) Yes. Tom Claburn (03:17) And they're trying to go out at two trillion now? Is that the number? Tobias Mann (03:25) Well, the number kind of depends on whether they're going to be able to sustain this. I was going to mention for the first time ever, their revenues outpaced their compute expenses two to one. This has never been true in the company's history, and it's one of the reasons that people are feeling more confident about this. The issue that really comes from all of this, and what has gotten missed somewhat in the more rosy interpretations of the S-1, is that they also are signed up to have to repay upwards of 800 billion dollars and counting of compute commitments out through the next two decades or so. Brandon (04:12) You outlined in your story just a whole host of people they owed billions of dollars to for compute. Like you said, it would be great. That $16.3 billion in [revenue] would be great if those compute costs were going to hold steady, right? But they're not. They're going to keep climbing and there are a lot of bills that are going to be due. So, profitability is relying on making more than that nearly trillion dollars in compute obligations, and that's a big if. Tom Claburn (04:43) I mean, the big question mark is in terms of what the technology does for inference costs, because I think a lot of this is betting on being able to get the same hardware that is much more efficient down the road and maybe not drop your prices proportionately and profit on the difference. I think the inference costs have dropped pretty significantly over the year, on average. I mean, it's really hard to calculate inference costs because there are so many different factors and it's really situational depending on the workload and how much caching is going on and things like that. But overall it's a lot cheaper to do inference now than it was a few months ago. Tobias Mann (05:34) Per token, yeah. Brandon (05:36) But again, I feel like if you're betting this $2 trillion IPO on the fact that we're going to keep getting better and cheaper at inference, right? I mean, I know Moore's Law is kind of a thing of the past, but at this point, what if we run up against another compute bottleneck and inference stops getting cheaper before they need it to? Obviously any IPO prospectus is one big document about risk, right? Like, "Hey, you might make a ton of money investing in this company, or we might go complete belly up and you lose everything," right? That's always a possibility. Tom Claburn (06:15) Right. And they still haven't demonstrated that the use case for AI is wide enough at volume that they claim it is. I mean, in certain sectors it's pretty obvious now there's going to be AI for a long time. Coding, everyone kind of agrees that works and we know how to manage that. And then there will be adjacent fields to that. But once you start getting into more general office work and regular business tasks that are not super-compute heavy, I don't know. It's a good question. We'll see if people are going to use it that broadly, but I just see it being overly optimistic. Tobias Mann (06:59) The big question I have right now is: Is there enough user demand to support even a $200 billion a year revenue stream? Because even going off just commitments that they can't get out of made in the first half of this year, that's $417 billion running out through about 2033 to 2036. Brandon (07:32) I think the upper end of your estimate was a total, including newer commitments, of about $807 billion. At the lower end, $782 billion at the lower end. That's not that much of a difference when you're looking at hundreds of billions of dollars. Tobias Mann (07:46) But if they can't

item.title: FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers
item.description: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday , the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange , the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals , which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024 . The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday , crypto exchange Bi

item.content:encoded: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday , the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange , the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals , which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024 . The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday , crypto exchange Bitget has now confirmed that the cyberattack where hackers drained $387.5 million worth of digital assets from the exchange’s wallets also has all the hallmarks of a North Korean operation. Its CEO did not go into too much detail, but did say that “IP behavioral patterns and on-chain signatures” suggest it was Kim’s cronies at work. This isn’t Binance's first expensive encounter with hackers, either. Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens. Four years later, the sums have grown considerably. Binance may have the reserves to make its customers whole, but the attackers responsible for the latest raid still have billions of dollars to launder. ®

item.title: Vintage fun: Prodding AI agents using retro hardware just because you can
item.description: From the department of "pointless but still cool" comes word of some kit being repurposed as a terminal for AI agents. AWS developer advocate Darko Mesaroš has connected a teletype to a modern command-line interface to revel in the delight of interacting with today's AI technology via a combination of a DECwriter and fanfold paper, or the display and keyboard of a computer whose heyday ended 40 years ago. Mesaroš' project involved AWS Kiro , a Command Line Interface (CLI) and agentic coding service. We would, however, contend that this is more about seeing what retro hardware can be made to do. Two problems needed solving: getting data to and from the teletype, and formatting the output to work on a piece of kit from another era of computing. He used Hayes modem emulation to deal with the serial connection, and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) for working with Kiro. Mesaroš used a WiModem232 for the former. The device emulates a standard Hayes-compatible modem and, according to Mesaroš, "Folks initially used this to connect Commodore 64s to BBSes in the modern era" (he started his computing journey with a Commodore 64). The latter, getting the Kiro CLI to work on a Teletype, was a little more complicated. Kiro's CLI isn't really suitable for a teleprinter capable of 30 characters per second, after all. A simple Rust application took Kiro's output (obtained via ACP) and turned it into something that a teletype, or dumb terminal, could handle. As we said, seemingly pointless, but making it work required knowledge of Rust, competence with containers, an understanding of ACP, and more than a little creative thinking. So, while one might argue it is pointless from a technical perspective, it is wonderfully educational otherwise. The repository is available and focuses on Kiro for obvious reasons (Mesaroš is an AWS developer advocate after all), but in a chat with The Register , Mesaroš said the concept was portable. He said, "Any coding assistant or any harness that supports ACP, this should work, right? I built it for Kiro, but it uses the standard ACP protocol, so I could easily plug in Claude Code or Codex. Anything that basically can serve as an ACP server should be perfectly fine. "Blessed be the standards, right?" There might be some issues. "The biggest problem with this thing is that it doesn't really handle packet drops at all," he explained. "Like, if you drop packets, they're just gone. There're no retries. It's just spitting information out." And then there is buffering. Or the lack of it. Mesaroš said, "There's actually no buffering happening here. Literally, it just comes down through the fire hose through this serial device, and the bottleneck itself is the serial device." Mesaroš had toyed with using the GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi, but settled on the serial device instead, since everything worked "out of the box." "It's kind of cheating," he admitted, "but it's also kind of good." Mesaroš collects vintage hardware, with a stash that ranges
item.dc:creator: Richard Speed
item.content:encoded: From the department of "pointless but still cool" comes word of some kit being repurposed as a terminal for AI agents. AWS developer advocate Darko Mesaroš has connected a teletype to a modern command-line interface to revel in the delight of interacting with today's AI technology via a combination of a DECwriter and fanfold paper, or the display and keyboard of a computer whose heyday ended 40 years ago. Mesaroš' project involved AWS Kiro , a Command Line Interface (CLI) and agentic coding service. We would, however, contend that this is more about seeing what retro hardware can be made to do. Two problems needed solving: getting data to and from the teletype, and formatting the output to work on a piece of kit from another era of computing. He used Hayes modem emulation to deal with the serial connection, and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) for working with Kiro. Mesaroš used a WiModem232 for the former. The device emulates a standard Hayes-compatible modem and, according to Mesaroš, "Folks initially used this to connect Commodore 64s to BBSes in the modern era" (he started his computing journey with a Commodore 64). The latter, getting the Kiro CLI to work on a Teletype, was a little more complicated. Kiro's CLI isn't really suitable for a teleprinter capable of 30 characters per second, after all. A simple Rust application took Kiro's output (obtained via ACP) and turned it into something that a teletype, or dumb terminal, could handle. As we said, seemingly pointless, but making it work required knowledge of Rust, competence with containers, an understanding of ACP, and more than a little creative thinking. So, while one might argue it is pointless from a technical perspective, it is wonderfully educational otherwise. The repository is available and focuses on Kiro for obvious reasons (Mesaroš is an AWS developer advocate after all), but in a chat with The Register , Mesaroš said the concept was portable. He said, "Any coding assistant or any harness that supports ACP, this should work, right? I built it for Kiro, but it uses the standard ACP protocol, so I could easily plug in Claude Code or Codex. Anything that basically can serve as an ACP server should be perfectly fine. "Blessed be the standards, right?" There might be some issues. "The biggest problem with this thing is that it doesn't really handle packet drops at all," he explained. "Like, if you drop packets, they're just gone. There're no retries. It's just spitting information out." And then there is buffering. Or the lack of it. Mesaroš said, "There's actually no buffering happening here. Literally, it just comes down through the fire hose through this serial device, and the bottleneck itself is the serial device." Mesaroš had toyed with using the GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi, but settled on the serial device instead, since everything worked "out of the box." "It's kind of cheating," he admitted, "but it's also kind of good." Mesaroš collects vintage hardware, with a stash that ranges from home computers made by Commodore and Sinclair, to a 1974 Data General Eclipse minicomputer and a plethora of Sun hardware. And, of course, an old Decwriter. He is also a dab hand with the soldering iron, having learned the skills to keep old hardware operational. Unlike today's equipment. "I have this big peeve over modern computers, where you just can't fix them," he said, "and it feels like such a waste of resources that when my MacBook dies I just have to drill a hole through it so nobody steals my data, and throw it away." As for Kiro-TTY – or accessing a coding assistant or agent over serial using a decades-old device – he wrote on his blog, "This absolutely serves no purpose." However, it did provide a novel way of working out how the ACP protocol worked. Perhaps not so usefully, it also taught the developer how to debug serial connectivity. "And in general it helps me stretch what I can do in the current age of AI coding, and keeps my curiosity alive." The destination might be pointless from a modern perspective, but the journey getting there is anything but. ®

item.title: From a life-changing garlic press to a super-glowy serum: 12 buys you’re loving right now
item.description: Casserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party season • Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Autumn, we’ve been expecting you. After a September that seemed to miss the memo about changing seasons, October made up for it with serial storms and nights that drew in faster than you could say “fall back”. Time to hunker down and, whisper it, even put the heating on – or at least fire up an electric heater if you’re still holding out on the radiators. But while you were drawn to the indoor pleasures of heaters, hot casseroles and hotter coffee , you’ve also had your eye on party season, or at least been thinking about venturing into those corners of your wardrobe that haven’t seen daylight since March. From a clothes steamer to breathe new life into your threads, a pencil skirt and sheer silk shirt to update your wardrobe, to a vitamin C serum to keep your skin glowing all winter, these were your favourite things in October. item.title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
item.description: Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal. The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official. Continue reading...

item.title: Microsoft's moolah mountain is more massive than ever. It just doesn't want the people who built it
item.description: Capitalism can seem so perverse. Take Microsoft, which is celebrating record financial performance by inviting 60,000 employees to consider continuing their careers outside the company . Voluntary redundancy may seem to make sense when a company's running out of cash, but Microsoft is dripping with the stuff . Redmond's first quarter for fiscal 2027 was a bonanza for the tech giant. Its Azure business is up over 48 percent y-o-y, revenues are through the roof, and it has so much moolah it returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases. This latter move probably soothed CEO Satya Nadella, who recently suffered, due to the vagaries of C-suite reimbursement and incentive packages, a 6 percent cut in his pocket money . But as he’s also a stockholder with about 0.01 percent of the company, his share of the cash return presumably eased the pain. He won't have been offered redundo. Jenkins, the large wheelbarrow if you please. Microsoft, then, can afford all its employees, each of whom contributed about $1.5 million to SatNad's bottom line in the last full fiscal year. The "massive efficiencies and RoI of AI" make a great line for a company flogging magic LLM juice, but the evidence remains elusive. AI is, of course, still the reason. Nothing else matters these days. It's just that it's not today's AI. Among all the fulsome figures it put on display for Q1 2027, analysts noted that Microsoft's capital expenditure wasn't as spendy as expected. Quite a lot has been pushed into next calendar year, not because it's not there to be spent – Microsoft could build a 1:1 scale model of the Vatican filled with robot priests if it wanted – but because so much it wanted to mash the Buy Now button for was "Out of stock. More expected soon." This is bad. MS added 88 datacenters in its most recent full financial year: fiscal 2026. That’s not enough datacenters for a cloud business expected to grow by half again in 2027, and hugely not enough to do the other thing. Lags in the cadence of deforestation, dewatering and detonation of the planet can't be tolerated. Thus there are contracts signed to get things back on track PDQ, with mucho, mucho, mucho sponduiks. In its most recent Q1 earnings call, Microsoft is hinting, those selfsame analysts say, that it will have to go to the debt market and go into " negative free cash flow " territory in 2028. In other words, as well as spending its own bank, the company will be taking out massive loans. This is why Billy and Bhavya Dev have to go. The cost of borrowing depends on the financial health of the borrower, and that boils down to how much profit you're making from the money you earn. A big round of redundancies, which are very costly in themselves, sits on the books of the year they happen. The hole in expenditure left by the vanished salaries lives on. The capital must flow. Will this work? Last week, we listed the reasons why it might not — price competition between rivals and incr

Nothing else matters these days. It's just that it's not today's AI. Among all the fulsome figures it put on display for Q1 2027, analysts noted that Microsoft's capital expenditure wasn't as spendy as expected. Quite a lot has been pushed into next calendar year, not because it's not there to be spent – Microsoft could build a 1:1 scale model of the Vatican filled with robot priests if it wanted – but because so much it wanted to mash the Buy Now button for was "Out of stock. More expected soon." This is bad. MS added 88 datacenters in its most recent full financial year: fiscal 2026. That’s not enough datacenters for a cloud business expected to grow by half again in 2027, and hugely not enough to do the other thing. Lags in the cadence of deforestation, dewatering and detonation of the planet can't be tolerated. Thus there are contracts signed to get things back on track PDQ, with mucho, mucho, mucho sponduiks. In its most recent Q1 earnings call, Microsoft is hinting, those selfsame analysts say, that it will have to go to the debt market and go into " negative free cash flow " territory in 2028. In other words, as well as spending its own bank, the company will be taking out massive loans. This is why Billy and Bhavya Dev have to go. The cost of borrowing depends on the financial health of the borrower, and that boils down to how much profit you're making from the money you earn. A big round of redundancies, which are very costly in themselves, sits on the books of the year they happen. The hole in expenditure left by the vanished salaries lives on. The capital must flow. Will this work? Last week, we listed the reasons why it might not — price competition between rivals and increasingly powerful local and open weight models, supply side shortages, you know the litany by now. This week is Groundhog week, with fresh stories singing the same songs from different choirs. Any sensible soul, especially developers sitting on the sharp end of AI's forcible insertion into their working lives, will know how uncertain the job market is. Voluntary redundancy is a very high stakes bet, and the game is very different if you're in an organization that's going downhill and may need to get rid of you later with far less cash available than if you're nominally making $1.5 million in a place whose biggest problem is that it physically can't move into a bigger shell. On average, only 5 percent or so of those offered voluntary redundancy take it, which Microsoft HR will have factored in. It's cold outside and snug within, so that may be on the high side. The biggest knock-on of such schemes is cultural, with only the very confident moving on out, a disproportionate loss of talent and role models. Hey, the cost of doing business, right? For those who do decide to leave and watch the fireworks from outside the tent, part of the deal is career development resources. Sounds great, if anyone knows what technical careers will look like if either AI works and does indeed do all the work, or it fails and the global financial system throws a humongous wobble. Or anything in between. So, here's an exercise in very dark humor quite fitting for the Halloween season. Ask your favorite AI what careers will be available for coders made redundant by AI. It will give you a long and plausible list. Then ask it – and yourself – why AI won't be able to do any of those jobs too. Buying a truck and a wrench and calling yourself a plumber is probably safest. Nobody will ever want AI to fix their toilet. ®

item.title: Britain's driverless dream hits a roundabout of awkward questions
item.description: As robotaxis continue trials in London, an independent research group thinks the UK needs to answer some serious questions before heading any further down the road. To kick off, the sovereignty question, or "Will Britain become dependent on autonomous vehicle services for any key activities and what fallback options will exist if a supplier fails or withdraws?" as the Institute for Driverless Transport (IfDT) puts it. Another question concerns employment: "To what extent does professional driving form part of the UK's employment safety net and how will this function be recreated if demand for professional drivers is significantly reduced?" The objective for IfDT — an independent UK research and convening body focused on the consequences of autonomous vehicles — is to cast the net a bit wider than simply thinking about whether the software is sufficient to navigate London’s wiggly streets and narrow alleys. The research draws on work with operators trying to bring AVs to London and the regulators responsible for policy. It also relied on more than 30 conversations with councils, operators, industry, unions, charities, insurers, lawyers and universities. James Hutt, IfDT co-founder, said: "What struck us most in the interviews was how far this reaches: into jobs, public services, the built environment and national resilience. The people who know those areas best are rarely part of the conversation about AVs. "Our next step is to bring funding and researchers together with the businesses and public bodies that need answers. If you can fund research or offer a place to test it, we would like to hear from you." In August, Transport for London (TfL) granted private hire licences to autonomous vehicle operators provided that a human driver is present during journeys. Wayve and Uber have since launched self-driving rides in the UK capital, with 15 electric Ford Mustangs, equipped with the Wayve AI driver, set to pick up passengers with a safety driver on board. UK company Wayve also demoed a Nissan LEAF , running the Wayve AI Driver using NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion with self-driving equipment built more closely into the car's design. IfDT points out that Waymo and Baidu are also preparing services for London, while Uber, Pony.ai and Verne have begun testing in Manchester. The research organization said UK authorities still need to answer a long list of questions in order to shape long-term infrastructure plans for local areas and prepare for AI's impact on the labor market. The question of who needs to do this also remains unanswered, as the IfDT asks: "Which are the key public bodies that should already be anticipating the impact of AVs on their own work and who within those organisations should lead a response?"®

item.title: From expertise to intelligence: NISCO deploys world's first swarm-intelligence steel model at scale
item.description: Nanjing Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. (NISCO) has worked with Huawei and ecosystem partners to commercially deploy the world's first steel model powered by swarm intelligence - the YuanYe Steel Large Model (YuanYe) - across multiple scenarios at scale. This helps NISCO transition its core operations from relying on experience to being powered by data and intelligence collaboration. As a traditional manufacturer navigating the challenges of transformation and cost efficiency, NISCO has built a robust digital and intelligent foundation by adopting industry-leading products including Ascend, Kunpeng, Huawei Cloud Stack, and Pangu models. By embedding AI into every core stage of production - ironmaking, steelmaking, rolling, and quality inspection - NISCO is forging green and high-end AI-powered super steel plants. Unlike general-purpose monolithic models, YuanYe innovatively fuses multiple AI models with the steel industry's metallurgical mechanism models to create a dual-drive, multi-model cluster architecture. This architecture features a "right brain" for probabilistic computing and a "left brain" for precise and scientific decision-making. Powered by massive amounts of sensing data aggregated from millions of operational technology (OT) data points across 26 business domains, NISCO has achieved real-time digital twin mapping within its intelligent operations center, laying solid data and scenario foundations for YuanYe. This enables the entire steelmaking process to become not only visible, but also capable of precise control and intelligent assessment. Now 100 percent of NISCO's key equipment is connected and digitally controlled and its new product R&D cycles have been shortened by 50 percent, reducing annual costs by over CNY100m (approx. US$15m). As the model continues to iterate, NISCO had launched 25 business agents by October 2026. These agents cover a wide range of scenarios, from visual quality inspection and process optimization to production scheduling and operations management, setting a new benchmark for digital and intelligent steel transformation. Breakthroughs in four core scenarios: YuanYe redefines traditional operations for significant safety, efficiency, and quality gains In the ironmaking stage, AI makes traditionally invisible blast furnaces transparent. YuanYe leverages blast furnaces' internal sensor data and metallurgical mechanism analysis to perform real-time dynamic simulations of the ironmaking process. Assisted by furnace temperature prediction and health diagnosis models, furnace operators can predict temperatures and identify issues two hours in advance, with over 90 percent accuracy. This shifts furnace operations from reactive post-event remediation to proactive pre-control, increasing prime-grade molten iron yield by over 10 percent while significantly cutting unit energy consumption. In the rolling stage, AI drives precise predictions and codifies expert experience to enhance the operational stability of steel rollin
item.dc:creator: Huawei
item.content:encoded: Nanjing Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. (NISCO) has worked with Huawei and ecosystem partners to commercially deploy the world's first steel model powered by swarm intelligence - the YuanYe Steel Large Model (YuanYe) - across multiple scenarios at scale. This helps NISCO transition its core operations from relying on experience to being powered by data and intelligence collaboration. As a traditional manufacturer navigating the challenges of transformation and cost efficiency, NISCO has built a robust digital and intelligent foundation by adopting industry-leading products including Ascend, Kunpeng, Huawei Cloud Stack, and Pangu models. By embedding AI into every core stage of production - ironmaking, steelmaking, rolling, and quality inspection - NISCO is forging green and high-end AI-powered super steel plants. Unlike general-purpose monolithic models, YuanYe innovatively fuses multiple AI models with the steel industry's metallurgical mechanism models to create a dual-drive, multi-model cluster architecture. This architecture features a "right brain" for probabilistic computing and a "left brain" for precise and scientific decision-making. Powered by massive amounts of sensing data aggregated from millions of operational technology (OT) data points across 26 business domains, NISCO has achieved real-time digital twin mapping within its intelligent operations center, laying solid data and scenario foundations for YuanYe. This enables the entire steelmaking process to become not only visible, but also capable of precise control and intelligent assessment. Now 100 percent of NISCO's key equipment is connected and digitally controlled and its new product R&D cycles have been shortened by 50 percent, reducing annual costs by over CNY100m (approx. US$15m). As the model continues to iterate, NISCO had launched 25 business agents by October 2026. These agents cover a wide range of scenarios, from visual quality inspection and process optimization to production scheduling and operations management, setting a new benchmark for digital and intelligent steel transformation. Breakthroughs in four core scenarios: YuanYe redefines traditional operations for significant safety, efficiency, and quality gains In the ironmaking stage, AI makes traditionally invisible blast furnaces transparent. YuanYe leverages blast furnaces' internal sensor data and metallurgical mechanism analysis to perform real-time dynamic simulations of the ironmaking process. Assisted by furnace temperature prediction and health diagnosis models, furnace operators can predict temperatures and identify issues two hours in advance, with over 90 percent accuracy. This shifts furnace operations from reactive post-event remediation to proactive pre-control, increasing prime-grade molten iron yield by over 10 percent while significantly cutting unit energy consumption. In the rolling stage, AI drives precise predictions and codifies expert experience to enhance the operational stability of steel rolling and secure leadership in product quality. To tackle the highly dynamic and complex operating conditions during the rolling process, YuanYe's rolling-force prediction model achieves millisecond-level response, narrowing the thickness tolerance to ±0.2 mm and reducing the steel thickness deviation to 1.9 percent to reach a world-leading standard. The rolling-force hit rate has jumped from 88 percent to 98 percent, supporting a steady annual output of over 2.5 million tons of steel plates and increasing the overall yield rate by 0.5 percent. Enhanced dimensional precision and physical-chemical stability allow NISCO's products to meet demanding steel specifications across diverse applications, ranging from mega stadiums and oil pipelines to 10,000-ton cruise ships and LNG storage tanks. In quality inspection, the synergy between robots and AI models serves as a discerning "eagle eye", doubling metallographic inspection efficiency. During metallographic inspection for finished steel, the integrated smart metallographic inspection system built on YuanYe has achieved full-process automation, covering sample grinding and polishing, image acquisition, and smart grading. Inspection accuracy has risen to over 95 percent, while per-sample inspection time has been shortened from 10 minutes down to 3–5 minutes. This 80 percent increase in overall inspection efficiency frees human operators to focus on anomaly analysis and high-level decision-making. In the energy and environmental control stage, NISCO leverages the YuanYe architecture to develop the S-Link Intelligent Agent for Gas and Flue Gas Sulfur Control. Integrating 602 process parameters alongside multi-modal image and knowledge capabilities, the agent achieves a smart closed loop across source prediction, process optimization, and end-of-pipe compliance. By combining mechanism inversion with time-series forecasting, it issues precise sulfur-risk warnings one hour in advance, achieving a sulfur prediction accuracy of over 95 percent. Operational optimization algorithms then calculate the optimal gas blending scheme within seconds. Finally, game-theoretic models dynamically allocate emission quotas, slashing natural gas co-firing consumption by nearly 50 percent. This has reduced downtime caused by emission exceedance by over 25 percent, and delivered more than CNY600,000 (approx. US$90,000) in annual economic benefits - securing both environmental compliance and drastic cost reduction. From automating labor to empowering people: Defining a new paradigm of inclusive AI Li Jinyan, General Manager of the Digital and Intelligent Integrated Development Department and Director of the AI Research Institute at NISCO, said: "Digital and intelligent transformation is inherently human-centric. Its purpose is not to replace people, but to unleash human potential. Our goal is to lift employees out of the endless sea of data, empowering them to direct their creative energy toward work of higher value." To date, NISCO has deployed over 300 AI models across its plants, alongside more than 1,000 low-code agents and lightweight applications built independently by frontline employees. As Cheng Yongfu, Senior Industrial Solution Expert at Huawei's Steel & Non-ferrous BU, noted: "The real value of industrial AI can only be realized when it expands from single-point applications to comprehensive integration with production, operations, and management, which can unlock sustained, scalable empowerment." Looking ahead, as model deployment expands and computing demands continue to grow, NISCO will team up with Huawei and other partners to explore the construction of dedicated data centers for smart steel plants. Centered on the AI-native three-tier architecture (AI-native OS, AI-native factory, and AI-native enterprise) and powered by the YuanYe model, NISCO is accelerating high-quality steel development, aiming to provide a replicable and scalable benchmark for the digital and intelligent transformation of the global steel and manufacturing industries. Supplied by Huawei

item.title: Manager threatened to fire a colleague, then gave them a critical task – which they flubbed
item.description: Welcome to Monday morning, an occasion The Register marks with a new instalment of " Who, Me? " It's our reader-contributed column in which you confess to workplace mistakes and share your escapes from subsequent scrapes. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Gordon" who told us he once worked as an engineer at a major semiconductor corporation. Gordon rose to become manager of an engineering team which worked on a very popular PC chipset. One of the chaps on this team wasn't pulling his weight, so Gordon got the job of telling him to improve, or leave. "In all fairness, he was a nice guy but not a great engineer and needed to be better," Gordon told The Register. Not long after that moment of managerial unpleasantness, Gordon's team got the job of doing a full backup of the chipset's "production stepping" – the silicon equivalent of a minor point release. The idea was to create a detailed record that could be used as a restore point. "This was not a nightly backup, but a purposeful backup to retain a snapshot of the entire cleaned-up design database for future cases where we might need to spin another stepping quickly," Gordon explained. Gordon told his underperforming colleague to do the backup. "Because I was overworked, I did not think this through," he told The Register . The at-risk worker quickly proved why he was under the pump by deciding the backup wasn't necessary until the team completed the next stepping – but didn't tell anyone about that plan. Before that next stepping was done, the employee's past indiscretions caught up with him and he was let go. The story now fast-forwards six years, to a moment when Gordon learned that a customer wanted to buy the old chipset design so they could make a radiation-hardened version to use on satellites. The major semiconductor company liked the sound of that, and asked Gordon to find the backup. "My colleague and I then pieced together what had happened," he wrote. "Being good engineers, we said nothing. We searched through old nightly backup tapes until we found bits and pieces of different steppings of the design database and copied them all to one place, then handed this off to the customer." To this day, Gordon doesn't know if the customer was able to produce a useful chip from the bits of backup he cobbled together. "Did they realize they received bits and pieces of two slightly different databases? Did they care? Was the project canceled before anyone realized it?" "From then on, I was more careful about who I assigned the task of creating restore backups for each design project," he told The Register . "And I kept a record of the emails requesting backups and confirmation that backups had been done." Have you given a job to the wrong person? Or given clients slightly dodgy data? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We would love to tell your tale on a future Monday. ®

item.title: Chap who coded Google’s Pac-Man clone reveals how the game freaked out Firefox
item.description: A designer named Marcin Wichary has revealed the story of how he freaked out a decent slab of the world’s Firefox-using population with Pac-Man. Wichary has held senior design roles at Figma, Medium, and Google. As he wrote here , in 2010 Google decided to celebrate the 30 th anniversary of Pac-Man by changing its logo at Google.com to a playable version of the game. The Google of 2010 could still mention its motto of the time, “Don’t be evil,” without making anyone who heard it guffaw incredulously. The company’s frequent changes to the logo on its homepage – called Google Doodles , and which persist to this day – were still a notable part of net culture. Wichary got the job of building the playable logo, and tweaking Pac-Man to replace its usual maze with a course that instead navigated around the letters GOOGLE. “It was, frankly, a terrifying proposition,” Wichary wrote. “The homepage was then a very important destination, and my job title was only adjacent to ‘software engineer.’ But I started researching the game and recreating it all in HTML and CSS." Google wanted a full Pac-Man experience, including sound, "because so many of Pac-Man’s sounds are beyond iconic: the starting melody, the waka-wakas, the death jingle." Wichary began work before Google sought permission from Pac-Man’s owner Namco, because the search giant was “planning to wow them with a close-to-finished doodle.” “The project was … going really well. I had fun coding the game and we seemed to have fun playing it. Namco eventually got onboard, too,” he wrote. Google liked the game work so much, higher-ups decided it would be a great idea to have it start automatically if visitors to google.com stayed idle for ten seconds. The designer liked that idea. “If there was anything scary about it at the time, it was only the thought of my code getting even more exposure – but I wasn’t worried about distraction, since the homepage was not a destination page you would ever linger on.” What Google didn’t realise was that some people lingered on the home page without ever knowing they were there. Those people used the Firefox browser with an extension called CoolPreviews that let users hover over a link to see a preview of a web page. “The extension would quietly start at the same time Firefox was opened,” Wichary explained. “And it would immediately, in the background, invisibly and unbeknownst to the user, open a website.” That website was Google’s home page, which now featured an auto-playing and version of Pac-Man that CoolPreviews users simply did not expect. Which explained why, not long after setting the Pac-Man doodle live, Google received plenty of praise, but also reports about computers making strange noises due to CoolPreviews invisibly opening the noisy game. “I pushed a patch within hours,” Wichary wrote, explaining that he added a mute button and a requirement to click something to make the game and its noises start. CoolPreviews couldn’t make those clicks, so the phantom

Wichary has held senior design roles at Figma, Medium, and Google. The Google of 2010 could still mention its motto of the time, “Don’t be evil,” without making anyone who heard it guffaw incredulously. Wichary began work before Google sought permission from Pac-Man’s owner Namco, because the search giant was “planning to wow them with a close-to-finished doodle.” “The project was … going really well. I had fun coding the game and we seemed to have fun playing it. Namco eventually got onboard, too,” he wrote. Google liked the game work so much, higher-ups decided it would be a great idea to have it start automatically if visitors to google.com stayed idle for ten seconds. The designer liked that idea. “If there was anything scary about it at the time, it was only the thought of my code getting even more exposure – but I wasn’t worried about distraction, since the homepage was not a destination page you would ever linger on.” What Google didn’t realise was that some people lingered on the home page without ever knowing they were there. Those people used the Firefox browser with an extension called CoolPreviews that let users hover over a link to see a preview of a web page. “The extension would quietly start at the same time Firefox was opened,” Wichary explained. “And it would immediately, in the background, invisibly and unbeknownst to the user, open a website.” That website was Google’s home page, which now featured an auto-playing and version of Pac-Man that CoolPreviews users simply did not expect. CoolPreviews couldn’t make those clicks, so the phantom Pac-Man sounds went away. “Ironically, I don’t believe we ever heard of normal people being bothered by the autoplay – it seemed that indeed, few people stayed on the homepage for 10 seconds doing absolutely nothing,” Wichary wrote. “The funny thing is that emergency live-patching [the] internet’s at the time most valuable homepage was perhaps the scariest part of that day for me, but that completely went over my sleep-deprived head,” he added. Google changed Wichary’s title after this incident. His post shows an image describing him as “User experience designer. The Michael Bay of doodles.” ®

item.title: India floats AI plan under which ‘The model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model’
item.description: As debate and legal argument continue over the extent to which developers of large language models are entitled to feed the world’s data into their systems without paying for it, India’s government has come up with an idea to regulate and secure the flow of information. India’s motive is to create AI models trained on local data, because it thinks offshore model-makers won’t be motivated to address the nation’s issues or to ensure owners of data stay in control. The scheme India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) thinks can make that happen is called the “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training.” As described by Professor Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, DEPA means “the model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model.” The scheme envisions “Training Data Providers” (TDPs) – examples of which include hospitals, banks, and government agencies – sharing anonymized and encrypted data with a “Data Exchange Platform” (DEP). Entities called “Training Data Consumers” (TDCs) access the data stored at the DEPs to train their models. DEPs will operate what MeitY calls “hardware-based Secure Data Environments” in which “data remains encrypted and isolated even during processing.” They also enforce rules set by TDPs that describe how TDCs can use data. MeitY’s DEPA framework [PDF] says this scheme means “Differential privacy techniques are systematically applied to prevent the model from learning or revealing individual specific information,” adding “All activities inside the secure data environments are immutably logged for audit purposes, ensuring that the process is both secure and transparent.” India’s government already operates several data exchanges, but it is unclear how much work remains to make DEPA a reality. Once DEPA is working, MeitY envisions model-makers will use it to do things like “unlock currently fragmented health data to power breakthroughs in AI-driven diagnostics, drug discovery, and public health management.” The optimism extends to financial services. India is home to literally thousands of banks, and MeitY thinks “DEPA can enable secure sharing of diverse financial data, potentially extending formal credit to 400 million underserved individuals and MSMEs and fueling next-generation fintech innovation.” India’s government has long believed that if financial services companies can lend to more people, it will boost economic development. “Similarly, in Education, DEPA can overcome data interoperability challenges to enable AI-powered personalized learning for millions and create portable skill credentials essential for a future-ready workforce of its 250 million students in a $29 billion EdTech sector,” the framework states. “The successful adoption of DEPA Training across these domains is the essential catalyst for realizing India’s vision of inclusive growth and responsible AI leadership on the global stage.” While t

The scheme India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) thinks can make that happen is called the “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI Training.” As described by Professor Ajay Kumar Sood, Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India, DEPA means “the model travels to the data, rather than the data travelling to the model.” The scheme envisions “Training Data Providers” (TDPs) – examples of which include hospitals, banks, and government agencies – sharing anonymized and encrypted data with a “Data Exchange Platform” (DEP). Entities called “Training Data Consumers” (TDCs) access the data stored at the DEPs to train their models. DEPs will operate what MeitY calls “hardware-based Secure Data Environments” in which “data remains encrypted and isolated even during processing.” They also enforce rules set by TDPs that describe how TDCs can use data. MeitY’s DEPA framework [PDF] says this scheme means “Differential privacy techniques are systematically applied to prevent the model from learning or revealing individual specific information,” adding “All activities inside the secure data environments are immutably logged for audit purposes, ensuring that the process is both secure and transparent.” India’s government already operates several data exchanges, but it is unclear how much work remains to make DEPA a reality. Once DEPA is working, MeitY envisions model-makers will use it to do things like “unlock currently fragmented health data to power breakthroughs in AI-driven diagnostics, drug discovery, and public health management.” The optimism extends to financial services. India is home to literally thousands of banks, and MeitY thinks “DEPA can enable secure sharing of diverse financial data, potentially extending formal credit to 400 million underserved individuals and MSMEs and fueling next-generation fintech innovation.” India’s government has long believed that if financial services companies can lend to more people, it will boost economic development. “Similarly, in Education, DEPA can overcome data interoperability challenges to enable AI-powered personalized learning for millions and create portable skill credentials essential for a future-ready workforce of its 250 million students in a $29 billion EdTech sector,” the framework states. “The successful adoption of DEPA Training across these domains is the essential catalyst for realizing India’s vision of inclusive growth and responsible AI leadership on the global stage.” While the purpose of the framework is to build Indian AIs for Indians, the document also has half an eye on the nation’s international standing. “DEPA is India’s contribution to global science diplomacy, advancing the efforts of institutions such as the World Bank and the United Nations to shape a more inclusive and responsible global AI ecosystem,” the framework states. It also makes several mentions of digital public infrastructure (DPI), an idea pioneered by India that involves government funding creation of tools like the Unified Payments Interface payment systems and the Bharat Taxi zero-commission ride-sharing platform, to ensure Big Tech companies don’t dominate the local market. India also uses its DPI as a diplomatic tool, by giving it away to friendly nations. ®

item.title: Google says Asian advertisers spending less due to Europe's customs changes
item.description: Google has revealed some of its Asian customers – almost certainly Chinese e-tailers – are buying fewer ads. Speaking on Alphabet’s Q3 earnings call last week, chief business officer Philipp Schindler addressed the slowdown in ad sales growth with the following remark: “In retail, some of our APAC advertisers were impacted by the EU eliminating its de minimis exemption.” That’s a reference to the European Union’s changes to import duties, which saw the bloc introduce a temporary €3 customs duty for every consignment valued at under €150 imported from outside the EU. The EU previously operated the de minimis exemption that Schindler referred to, meaning it collected no import duty on almost 5.9 billion low-value items shipped to the continent in 2025 alone. The new regime aims to protect European retailers from cheap imports. A great many of those items came from Chinese e-tail giants – the likes of Temu, Shein, and Alibaba – who are thought to account for perhaps ten percent of advertising revenue at Google and Meta. EU policy has therefore contributed to slower growth at Google. Huawei’s brake pedals reportedly break Huawei’s automotive efforts appear to have driven it into a cul de sac of controversy. The Chinese tech giant works with a company called Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group Co. (JAC) under the Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance , which aims to produce intelligent cars. The flagship model produced by Huawei and JAC is a luxury EV called the Maextro V800, which when tested by Chinese automotive review site Dongchedi produced a rather terrifying fault: the brake pedal bracket broke when drivers exerted maximum force during tests to assess the car's ability to decelerate suddenly at 100 km/h. The site’s drivers were still able to stop the car, but rather more slowly than is optimal. Within days of the review site posting its findings, reports of its work started to disappear from the internet, according to China Digital Times , a US-based outlet that says it publishes independent news on Chinese affairs. Even some opinion pieces that called for further assessment of the car’s safety disappeared, giving rise to theories that Beijing is displeased with negative coverage of its technology champions and automotive industry. item.content:encoded: Google has revealed some of its Asian customers – almost certainly Chinese e-tailers – are buying fewer ads. Speaking on Alphabet’s Q3 earnings call last week, chief business officer Philipp Schindler addressed the slowdown in ad sales growth with the following remark: “In retail, some of our APAC advertisers were impacted by the EU eliminating its de minimis exemption.” That’s a reference to the European Union’s changes to import duties, which saw the bloc introduce a temporary €3 customs duty for every consignment valued at under €150 imported from outside the EU. The EU previously operated the de minimis exemption that Schindler referred to, meaning it collected no import duty on almost 5.9 billion low-value items shipped to the continent in 2025 alone. The new regime aims to protect European retailers from cheap imports. A great many of those items came from Chinese e-tail giants – the likes of Temu, Shein, and Alibaba – who are thought to account for perhaps ten percent of advertising revenue at Google and Meta. EU policy has therefore contributed to slower growth at Google. Huawei’s brake pedals reportedly break Huawei’s automotive efforts appear to have driven it into a cul de sac of controversy. The Chinese tech giant works with a company called Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group Co. (JAC) under the Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance , which aims to produce intelligent cars. The flagship model produced by Huawei and JAC is a luxury EV called the Maextro V800, which when tested by Chinese automotive review site Dongchedi produced a rather terrifying fault: the brake pedal bracket broke when drivers exerted maximum force during tests to assess the car's ability to decelerate suddenly at 100 km/h. The site’s drivers were still able to stop the car, but rather more slowly than is optimal. Within days of the review site posting its findings, reports of its work started to disappear from the internet, according to China Digital Times , a US-based outlet that says it publishes independent news on Chinese affairs. Even some opinion pieces that called for further assessment of the car’s safety disappeared, giving rise to theories that Beijing is displeased with negative coverage of its technology champions and automotive industry. North Korea named as Binance hacker The USA’s Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Saturday named North Korea’s elite cybercrime crew “TraderTraitor” as the source of last week’s attack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance . Cyber-defense company TRM also reached the same conclusion. Its analysts last week declared they have “high confidence” that “on and off-chain intelligence” suggest TraderTraitor did the deed. “On the evening of October 29, billions of dollars in crypto began leaving wallets belonging to Binance,” TRM’s analysts wrote. “Within minutes, Binance wallets on the XRP Ledger, Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana and four other networks had sent their balances to addresses controlled by a single attacker. A second wave around 23:05 UTC reached Binance wallets on Avalanche and Polygon.” TRM thinks Trader Traitor started its raid 36 hours before the theft. “The attacker's operator wallet received three small withdrawals from Tornado Cash, a service that obscures where crypto comes from, starting the morning of October 28,” TRM wrote. “Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets. Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Binance first said the cause of the incident was a single compromised laptop. It has since detected “additional points of breach” but has not offered additional information while it investigates the matter. The crypto exchange continues to reassure users that its platform is safe and that it will make good any losses. North Korea steals cryptocurrency to fund its government, especially its belligerent defense efforts. Samsung posts monster profit Samsung last week delivered the monster profits it promised early in October. The Korean giant announced record Q3 revenue of ₩195.3 trillion ($146.2 billion ) and operating profit of ₩107 trillion ($80 billion). Samsung’s DS division, which covers all its chipmaking efforts, earned over 99 percent of that operating profit and $110 billion of the company’s revenue. The company said its foundry business “experienced a notable revenue and earnings improvement on HBM base-die sales growth” and expects it will notch up “double-digit revenue growth and continued earnings improvement on new mobile products, mass production ramp-up of 4nm NPUs, and expanded memory product sales” in its next quarterly report. “In 2027, the Business will aim for revenue growth led by 4nm and 2nm advanced nodes based on strong AI and HPC demand. It also expects to strengthen its global supply capabilities with the commencement of operations at its new fab in Taylor, Texas,” the company said. That last item is welcome news as the reason Samsung and other memory-makers are making so much money is shortages mean they can inflate prices. More factories coming online may help to ease price pressures. Fast-charging batteries set for takeoff Dr Rachid Yazami, the scientist who developed the graphite anode that made lithium-ion batteries mainstream, has shown off a new battery design that can achieve 70 percent charge in under four minutes. In tests of its lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell, Dr Yazami’s startup KVI was able to go from 10 percent to 70 percent charge in 3.7 minutes, and to full charge in seven minutes, using “Non-Linear Voltammetry (NLV)” technology that he says “uses a proprietary, stepwise voltage-controlled approach” that “allows the current to respond to the battery’s changing electrochemical characteristics” during charging. “The challenge is not simply to push more electricity into a battery in less time,” Dr Yazami said. “It is to understand how the battery responds during charging and use that information to deliver energy more effectively.” Japanese company SkyDrive, which hopes to manufacture electric-powered flying vehicles, has signed up to test the tech. ®

item.title: Linus Torvalds says Linux kernel is out of 'stabilization phase' and using 'much healthier model' for AI contributions
item.description: Linus Torvalds has posted the first release candidate for version 7.4 of the Linux kernel and offered his opinion that the project has found a “much healthier model” for using AI. “This is a *BIG* merge window,” he wrote in his weekly state of the kernel update , as it contains almost 20,000 commits compared to the usual ~15,000 that developers submit for a new cut of the kernel. “I think the reason is the by now obvious one, but I'm actually taking it as a good sign: I'm *much* happier with the flood of AI triggered work going into the merge window than it showing up mainly as extra fixes during the -rc period.” He therefore hopes that the unusually large number of commits “is a sign that the AI fixes are becoming more part of the ‘normal development’ than a flood of fixes that go into the whole stabilization phase." “I think that's a much healthier model,” he added, before hedging with the observation that “people are expecting 7.4 to be the next LTS [long-term support] release, which is another independent reason why some releases tend larger than others.” “So it may not *just* be the flood of AI patches.” Torvalds also seems not to be completely convinced that all AI submissions are entirely helpful, by describing this release as “Large, and full of fixes for issues found by AI (and more and more the patches have been suggested by AI too, although they often get rewritten).” AMD GPU register offsets and bit masks make up a third of the changes this time around. “We've been here before, and I'm sure we'll see it many times again in the future,” Torvalds wrote. “Just ignore the noise.” The kernel-watchers at Phoronix rate the major inclusions in Linux 7.4 as improved support for processors from AMD, Apple, and Google. Other additions include some handy tweaks to improve security for virtual machines, support for the Raspberry Pi 10-inch monitor and more work to get Linux running happily on Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 SoC for PCs. ®

item.title: Why you should treat charisma as a red flag
item.description: Today’s crop of smooth talkers tap directly into a specific evolutionary vulnerability. Here’s how to defend yourself Recently, I was alone in a bar waiting for a friend. To pass the time, I started chatting to a stranger. He had an easy, confident way of speaking, which I admired. We discussed topics I know little about: the instability of modern economies, the feasibility of commercial space travel, the likelihood of a coup in Russia. I found myself leaning in and asking questions: I felt as if I could learn a lot from this person. We eventually got to psychology, which is more my wheelhouse. I brooded about how easy it’s become for people to accept strange ideas. “Some people will believe anything,” he observed. “Some people even believe the Earth is round !” It’s increasingly difficult to ignore how fragmented and bizarre our beliefs have become. We live in our own echo chambers, defined by the channels, feeds and influencers we follow. As a result we can arrive at very polarised conclusions about vaccines, the climate, gender, geopolitics, the shape of the Earth and everything else. Disagreements on topics like these frequently damage relationships, alienate friends and estrange loved ones. Continue reading...

item.title: 'Mother of all editors' Emacs is 50
item.description: No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab. Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more: "How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement." There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for " E diting MAC ro S ", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy died earlier this year at the age of 83. The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs . It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge ). As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976 . (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.) This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says: "RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet." RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development. Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs , last updated in 2020. Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008 , RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August. Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an ess
